topic: Functional areas, Incident Commander and Command Staff

notes.front: What is the Intelligence/Investigations (I/I) function?
notes.back: A sixth ICS function identified in NIMS, established for incidents with intensive intelligence gathering and investigative activity.
notes.explanation: It is not a default part of the five functional areas; it is added only when an incident needs it, such as a criminal or terrorist act.
notes.example: Like standing up a dedicated I/I function for a suspected arson fire, but not for a routine structure fire.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 5, SM-p80

notes.front: What is Command, as NIMS defines it?
notes.back: The act of directing, ordering or controlling by virtue of explicit statutory, regulatory or delegated authority.
notes.explanation: This is the legal basis every Incident Commander’s authority rests on.
notes.example: Like a fire chief’s statutory authority to order an evacuation.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Incident Command, as an ICS organizational element?
notes.back: The ICS element responsible for overall management of the incident: the Incident Commander or Unified Command, plus any Command Staff activated.
notes.explanation: It names the whole top block of the ICS chart, not just the one person leading it.
notes.example: Like the "head office" of the incident: the Incident Commander plus whichever Command Staff have been assigned.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is the Incident Commander (IC) responsible for?
notes.back: On-scene incident activities, including developing objectives and ordering and releasing resources, with overall authority and responsibility.
notes.explanation: Every other role in ICS ultimately answers to, or exists to support, this one position.
notes.example: Like the one person at a structure fire who sets the plan and controls which resources are called in or released.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is a Deputy, in ICS terms?
notes.back: Someone fully qualified to replace a superior, delegated their authority; assignable to the IC, an Emergency Operations Center director, General Staff, or branch director.
notes.explanation: A Deputy must be as qualified as the person they could relieve, which is the one hard requirement ICS sets for the role.
notes.example: Like a fully qualified Deputy IC who can step in seamlessly if the IC needs rest.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Who makes up the Command Staff?
notes.back: Personnel the IC or Unified Command assigns to support command: usually a Public Information Officer, Safety Officer and Liaison Officer, reporting to the IC.
notes.explanation: These roles support command itself; additional positions may be added, distinct from the General Staff, which runs the four functional Sections.
notes.example: Like a small team advising and supporting the IC directly, rather than running a section of their own.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the ICS title "Officer" mean?
notes.back: The ICS title for a member of the Command Staff authorized to make decisions and act in their area of responsibility.
notes.explanation: It is the generic title the three Command Staff roles all share, before each gets its own specific title.
notes.example: Like calling any of the Public Information Officer, Safety Officer or Liaison Officer simply "an Officer" when speaking generally.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Public Information Officer (PIO) do?
notes.back: Interfaces with the public, media and other agencies that have incident-related information needs.
notes.explanation: The PIO is the single voice for information leaving the incident; IS-200.c notes the IC or Unified Command designates one as the lead PIO.
notes.example: Like the person who gives the press briefings and answers media calls about a wildfire.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary; IS-0200.c Student Manual, Lesson 4, Command Staff Responsibilities table, SM-p117

notes.front: What does the Safety Officer do?
notes.back: Monitors incident operations and advises the IC or Unified Command on all matters of operational safety, including personnel health and safety.
notes.explanation: The Safety Officer can stop or prevent unsafe acts directly, which is a stronger power than "advising" alone suggests.
notes.example: Like the person who halts a crew entering an unstable structure until it is shored up.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What does the Liaison Officer do?
notes.back: Serves as the point of contact for representatives of cooperating and assisting agencies and organizations.
notes.explanation: The Liaison Officer is the outward-facing contact for other agencies, distinct from the PIO’s outward-facing contact for the public and media.
notes.example: Like the person a mutual-aid agency calls first when they arrive to offer help.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is Coordination, in ICS terms?
notes.back: Activities ensuring the on-site ICS organization gets the information, resources and support it needs — e.g. setting priorities among incidents.
notes.explanation: It supports the scene from outside the on-scene command, and the two are easy to confuse.
notes.example: Like an Emergency Operations Center resolving which of three simultaneous incidents gets a scarce helicopter first.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 26, SM-p105

notes.front: What is an Emergency Operations Center (EOC)?
notes.back: The physical, or virtual, location where coordination of information and resources to support on-scene incident management normally takes place.
notes.explanation: It relieves the IC of external coordination and resource-securing, so the IC can focus on the scene itself.
notes.example: Like a city’s dedicated room where multiple agencies coordinate resources for an ongoing flood.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What is a Joint Information Center (JIC)?
notes.back: A facility where personnel coordinate incident-related public information; the central point of contact for all news media.
notes.explanation: It is a place, unlike the PIO, who is a person; several agencies’ PIOs may co-locate there.
notes.example: Like a shared media center set up during a major hurricane response.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Which of the five major ICS functional areas: sets the incident objectives, strategies and priorities, and has overall responsibility for the incident?
notes.back: Incident Command.
notes.explanation: These five functional areas are the foundation every ICS organization is built on, whatever the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 4, SM-p79

notes.front: Which of the five major ICS functional areas: conducts operations to reach the incident objectives; establishes tactics and directs all operational resources?
notes.back: Operations.
notes.explanation: These five functional areas are the foundation every ICS organization is built on, whatever the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 4, SM-p79

notes.front: Which of the five major ICS functional areas: supports the incident action planning process by tracking resources, collecting/analyzing information, and maintaining documentation?
notes.back: Planning.
notes.explanation: These five functional areas are the foundation every ICS organization is built on, whatever the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 4, SM-p79

notes.front: Which of the five major ICS functional areas: arranges resources and needed services to support achievement of the incident objectives?
notes.back: Logistics.
notes.explanation: These five functional areas are the foundation every ICS organization is built on, whatever the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 4, SM-p79

notes.front: Which of the five major ICS functional areas: monitors costs related to the incident and provides accounting, procurement, time recording and cost analyses?
notes.back: Finance/Administration.
notes.explanation: These five functional areas are the foundation every ICS organization is built on, whatever the incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 4, SM-p79

notes.front: Which ICS position is always staffed, at every incident?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — on small incidents, the IC alone may perform every management function.
notes.explanation: No other ICS position is guaranteed to exist; the IC is the one constant.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 13, SM-p89

notes.front: Should IC qualification be based on rank or seniority?
notes.back: No — qualification should not be based solely on rank, grade or technical knowledge.
notes.explanation: ICS separates incident-command competence from an individual’s everyday organizational rank.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 12, SM-p88

notes.front: Name the IC’s three specific responsibilities, beyond overall incident management?
notes.back: Ensuring overall incident safety; providing information to stakeholders; establishing and maintaining liaison with other agencies.
notes.explanation: These three are named on top of the IC’s general management responsibility for the whole incident.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 15, SM-p91

notes.front: Who performs an ICS function that has not been delegated to a Section?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — the IC only creates sections that are needed, and is responsible for every function until it is delegated.
notes.explanation: This is why a small incident can run with only an IC and no Section Chiefs at all.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 19, SM-p97

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves a more qualified Incident Commander arriving?
notes.back: A more qualified Incident Commander arrives and assumes command.
notes.explanation: Transfer is a normal, expected part of an expanding or lengthy incident, for any of these four reasons.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 16, SM-p92

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves a law requiring a specific agency to take charge?
notes.back: An agency is legally required to take command (e.g., the FBI for terrorism investigations).
notes.explanation: Transfer is a normal, expected part of an expanding or lengthy incident, for any of these four reasons.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 16, SM-p92

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves the incident growing or spreading?
notes.back: The incident changes in complexity.
notes.explanation: Transfer is a normal, expected part of an expanding or lengthy incident, for any of these four reasons.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 16, SM-p92

notes.front: Which reason for transferring command involves the current Incident Commander needing rest?
notes.back: The current Incident Commander needs rest.
notes.explanation: Transfer is a normal, expected part of an expanding or lengthy incident, for any of these four reasons.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 16, SM-p92

notes.front: What are the five actions in properly assuming command of an incident already in progress?
notes.back: Assess with the current IC; get a face-to-face briefing; choose a transfer time; notify headquarters and staff; consider reassigning the previous IC.
notes.explanation: This ordered procedure ensures nothing from the previous IC’s knowledge is lost at handover.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 17, SM-p94

notes.front: Does a transfer of command on an expanding incident reflect badly on the outgoing IC?
notes.back: No — it is to be expected and does not reflect on the current Incident Commander’s competency.
notes.explanation: This reassures learners that handovers are routine, not a sign of failure.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 17, SM-p94

notes.front: Which of the four areas of incident management saves lives, stabilises the incident and protects property, and is carried out through ICS?
notes.back: Direct tactical response.
notes.explanation: These four areas, together, are how NIMS organizes command and coordination at every level.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 27, SM-p106

notes.front: Which of the four areas of incident management provides resources, information and interagency coordination, and is carried out through EOCs?
notes.back: Incident support.
notes.explanation: These four areas, together, are how NIMS organizes command and coordination at every level.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 27, SM-p106

notes.front: Which of the four areas of incident management gives senior-level policy guidance, and is carried out through Multiagency Coordination Groups?
notes.back: Policy guidance.
notes.explanation: These four areas, together, are how NIMS organizes command and coordination at every level.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 27, SM-p106

notes.front: Which of the four areas of incident management keeps the media and public informed, and is carried out through the Joint Information System?
notes.back: Outreach and communication.
notes.explanation: These four areas, together, are how NIMS organizes command and coordination at every level.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 27, SM-p106

notes.front: Does an ICS position title have to match someone’s everyday job title?
notes.back: No — there is no correlation between the ICS organization and any agency’s administrative structure; deployed staff use their ICS title.
notes.explanation: This is deliberate: mixing everyday titles into ICS caused confusion in the incidents ICS was built to fix.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 11, SM-p86/87

notes.front: Can an IC appoint advisors outside the standard Command Staff roles?
notes.back: Yes — the IC may appoint technical specialists, such as legal, medical, or access and functional needs experts, as command advisors.
notes.explanation: The IC can add expert advisors as command advisors without making them members of the Command Staff.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 20, SM-p98

notes.front: An arson investigation at a large fire needs dedicated intelligence-gathering and investigative work. Should this always run inside the standard five functional areas, unchanged?
notes.back: Not necessarily — Intelligence/Investigations can be stood up as a sixth ICS function for incidents like this.
notes.explanation: This tests recognising when I/I applies, not just its definition.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 5, SM-p80

notes.front: An IC with delegated authority orders an evacuation zone set up. What NIMS term names this act?
notes.back: Command — directing by virtue of explicit statutory, regulatory or delegated authority.
notes.explanation: This links the abstract legal definition to a concrete act of authority.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: An IC has appointed a Safety Officer and a PIO. What ICS element now includes the IC plus these two Officers?
notes.back: Incident Command — the IC or UC, plus any Command Staff activated.
notes.explanation: This tests that "Incident Command" names a whole element, not just the individual IC.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: At a small residential fire, no Section Chiefs have been appointed. Who is responsible for ordering and releasing resources?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — responsible for on-scene activities including ordering and releasing resources.
notes.explanation: This reinforces that resource authority sits with the IC even when no sections exist yet.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary
notes.choices:
A) The Incident Commander
B) The Safety Officer
C) Dispatch, since they control resource lists
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Safety Officer advises on safety but does not hold incident-wide resource authority. C: dispatch sends resources on request but does not hold incident authority to order or release them.

notes.front: An IC appoints an assistant who is not yet fully qualified to run the incident alone. Does this person meet the ICS definition of Deputy?
notes.back: No — a Deputy must be fully qualified and capable of assuming the position if needed.
notes.explanation: This tests the one firm qualification requirement for the Deputy role.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: An IC appoints a PIO, a Safety Officer and a Liaison Officer, all reporting directly to the IC. What group do they form together?
notes.back: The Command Staff.
notes.explanation: This links the three named roles to the collective term for them.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: What ICS title do the PIO, Safety Officer and Liaison Officer all share?
notes.back: Officer — the ICS title for Command Staff members authorised to act in their area of responsibility.
notes.explanation: This ties the general title to the authority every Command Staff member holds in their own lane.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Several agencies’ press officers are all giving different figures to reporters at the same incident. What ICS role and rule prevents this?
notes.back: A single lead Public Information Officer, approved by the IC/UC, coordinates all released information.
notes.explanation: This is a direct, concrete case of why the PIO role and single point of contact matter.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary
notes.choices:
A) A single lead PIO coordinating the message
B) Each agency should keep briefing separately for speed
C) The Safety Officer should take over media duties
notes.choicesExplained: B: separate uncoordinated briefings is exactly the failure described. C: the Safety Officer’s role is operational safety, not public information.

notes.front: A crew is about to enter a structure with a visibly unstable roof. Who has the authority to stop them?
notes.back: The Safety Officer — who can modify or stop the work of personnel to prevent unsafe acts.
notes.explanation: This tests that the Safety Officer’s power is not only advisory.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A mutual-aid crew arrives at an incident and needs a single point of contact to get oriented. Who should they ask for?
notes.back: The Liaison Officer — the point of contact for representatives of cooperating and assisting agencies.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes the Liaison Officer’s inter-agency role from the PIO’s public/media role.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: An EOC resolves which of two ongoing incidents gets a scarce helicopter first. Is this Command or Coordination?
notes.back: Coordination — it is about resource priorities across incidents, not directing on-scene tactics.
notes.explanation: This tests the boundary between Command (on scene) and Coordination (off scene, cross-incident).
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 26, SM-p105

notes.front: A Multiagency Coordination Group is meeting to set high-level policy priorities across three ongoing incidents. Which of the four overarching areas of incident management is this?
notes.back: Policy guidance and senior-level decision making.
notes.explanation: This links a specific coordinating body (Multiagency Coordination Group) to its named role among the four.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 27, SM-p106

notes.front: A city sets up a dedicated room where several agencies coordinate resources for an unfolding flood, away from the flood site itself. What is this?
notes.back: An Emergency Operations Center (EOC).
notes.explanation: This links the abstract definition to the physical, everyday example of an EOC.
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: Several agencies’ PIOs set up in one shared facility to handle all media inquiries about a hurricane. Is this a JIC or an EOC?
notes.back: A JIC — a Joint Information Center coordinates public information, not resources.
notes.explanation: This distinguishes JIC (public information) from EOC (resource and information coordination).
notes.source: NIMS 2017 Glossary

notes.front: A city’s public works director is deployed to an incident and assigned as a Division Supervisor. Should they use the title "Director" or "Division Supervisor" on the incident?
notes.back: "Division Supervisor" — the ICS title for the position they are assigned to, not their everyday job title.
notes.explanation: This applies the "no correlation with everyday titles" rule to a concrete case.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 11, SM-p86/87

notes.front: An IC is briefing agency executives and disaster survivors on the incident’s status. Which of the IC’s specific responsibilities is this?
notes.back: Providing information services to internal and external stakeholders.
notes.explanation: This links one of the IC’s three named responsibilities to a concrete briefing scenario.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 15, SM-p90

notes.front: A house fire spreads overnight into forest and neighbouring towns, crossing several jurisdictions. What is the most likely reason command would be transferred here?
notes.back: The incident changes in complexity.
notes.explanation: This tests picking the right reason for transfer from a described situation.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 16, SM-p92
notes.choices:
A) The incident changes in complexity
B) The current IC asked for a promotion
C) A new agency simply wants to be in charge
notes.choicesExplained: B: transfer of command is not about career advancement. C: wanting command is not itself a recognised reason; legal requirement, complexity, more-qualified arrival, or rest are the recognised reasons.

notes.front: An incoming IC accepts command without ever being briefed face-to-face by the outgoing IC. What step of the transfer procedure was skipped?
notes.back: Receiving an adequate briefing, ideally face-to-face, from the current IC.
notes.explanation: This is the specific, most consequential step in the five-action transfer procedure.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 17, SM-p94

notes.front: What is the difference between Command and Coordination in ICS?
notes.back: Command: on-scene — sets objectives, makes assignments, orders resources. Coordination: off-scene — shares information, synchronizes messages, sets priorities among incidents.
notes.explanation: Both direct incident work, but Command acts on scene while Coordination supports the scene from outside it, through Emergency Operations Centers, Multiagency Coordination Groups and the Joint Information System.
notes.contrast: Command directs the incident itself; Coordination supplies and synchronizes what the incident needs from outside it.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 30, SM-p109

notes.front: A new responder is told to give tactical progress reports to Operations and submit receipts to Finance/Administration. Which two of the five major ICS functional areas are named here?
notes.back: Operations and Finance/Administration.
notes.explanation: This applies the five functional areas to a concrete, everyday reporting situation.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 3, SM-p78

notes.front: A tiny incident has no Section Chiefs and no Command Staff at all. Is there still one ICS position guaranteed to be staffed?
notes.back: Yes — the Incident Commander, who may perform every management function alone on a small incident.
notes.explanation: This tests that the IC is the one constant even when every other position is absent.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 13, SM-p89

notes.front: A jurisdiction assigns its most senior-ranking officer as IC purely because of their rank, without regard to ICS experience. Does this follow ICS qualification guidance?
notes.back: No — IC qualification should not be based solely on rank, grade or technical knowledge.
notes.explanation: This applies the rule to a common real-world temptation: promoting by seniority alone.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 12

notes.front: An incident has grown, but the IC has only delegated Operations so far, leaving Planning, Logistics and Finance/Administration undelegated. Who currently performs those three functions?
notes.back: The Incident Commander — responsible for every ICS function until it is delegated.
notes.explanation: This extends the rule to a partially-delegated incident, not just a fully undelegated one.
notes.source: IS-0100.c Student Manual, Lesson 3, Visual 19
